results.name: Commercial Court CMC
results.question: How does the Commercial Court handle case management conferences?

unfiltered.answer:
In the Commercial Court, a mandatory Case Management Conference (CMC) should be fixed as promptly as possible, allowing time for preparatory steps, especially disclosure directions. [7]

If proceedings started by a Part 7 claim form, the claimant must take steps to fix the CMC within 14 days of all defendants who intend to defend having filed and served their defences. [7]

If proceedings started by a Part 8 claim form, the claimant must take steps to fix the CMC within 14 days of all defendants who wish to serve evidence having done so. [7]

If proceedings were transferred to the Commercial Court, the claimant must apply for a CMC within 14 days of the transfer order, unless the Judge already held or directed a CMC when making the transfer order. [7]

If the claimant fails to apply as required, any other party may apply for a CMC. [8]

The CMC is a very significant stage, and parties are encouraged to agree directions in advance, but attendance may still be required even where all proposed directions are agreed. [11]

If all proposed directions are agreed, a proposed consent order should be filed as soon as possible with a covering letter explaining any reason why attendance should not be required. [11]

Where directions are not agreed, the general rule in the Commercial Court is that the CMC will be an oral hearing. [11]

An oral hearing may exceptionally be dispensed with if the issues are straightforward and the cost of an oral hearing cannot be justified. [11]

If the parties want the CMC dealt with on documents, they must provide the required documents by 12 noon on the Tuesday of the week when the CMC is fixed for Friday, and that timing will be strictly enforced. [11]

Those documents include the case management bundle with completed information sheets, a draft order, a draft list of common ground and issues, and a signed statement from each advocate addressing the issues considered, any NDR steps or plans, and an estimate for trial time including reading time. [11]

Cases involving expert evidence or preliminary issues are ordinarily unlikely to be suitable for a CMC on documents. [11]

The Civil Procedure Rules also say that, in multi-track cases, the court may fix a CMC after allocation, and a representative familiar with the case and with sufficient authority must attend if the party has legal representation. [4][5]

If you want, I can also give you the Commercial Court’s rules on what directions are usually dealt with at the CMC.

results.name: Chancery Trial Bundles
results.question: What is the Chancery Guide's approach to trial bundles?

unfiltered.answer:
The Chancery Guide says trial documents must be filed in one or more bundles, including bundles of authorities, prepared in accordance with Appendix X. [1]

It says parties should minimise paper and, unless the court specifically requests otherwise, only electronic trial bundles should be lodged for the court’s use. [3]

Appendix X says no hard copy bundles should be filed with the court unless requested by the judge, and the parties should minimise use of hard copy bundles and documents. [8]

The claimant’s legal representative is responsible for preparing and providing the agreed trial bundles, unless the claimant is unrepresented and the court directs another party to do it. [2]

The Guide says preparing bundles requires a high level of co-operation between all legal representatives, and litigants in person must also co-operate. [2]

Where the volume and nature of the case make it sensible, a separate core bundle may be prepared for trial, containing the documents likely to be referred to most frequently. [5]

The core bundle should be separately paginated, and unless the court directs otherwise, it should be filed both electronically and in hard copy, with the two versions identical. [5]

If you want, I can also summarise the Chancery Guide’s Appendix X bundle requirements in a shorter checklist.

results.name: Patents Court Disclosure
results.question: What do the Patents Court rules say about disclosure?

unfiltered.answer:
In the Patents Court, parties are obliged to provide disclosure in accordance with CPR Part 31, as modified by Rule 63.9, PD 63.6.1–6.3, and Practice Direction 51U. [2]

The Patents Court Guide also says the claimants and defendants must make and serve a list in Form N265 of the documents in their possession, custody or control that they are required to disclose under standard disclosure, as modified by paragraph 5 of the Practice Direction for patents cases supplementing Part 63. [1]

It also says disclosure on identified issues may be limited to the documents or categories of documents listed in the relevant schedule. [1]

Under CPR Part 31, disclosure means stating that a document exists or has existed. [5]

CPR Part 31 also provides that a party to whom a document has been disclosed has a right to inspect it, subject to the stated exceptions. [6]

Practice Direction 31A says standard disclosure requires a reasonable search, a list of the documents the party is aware of that fall within the rule 31.6 categories and are or have been in the party’s control, and that the list should be in Form N265. [8][9][11]

The available sources do not give the full text of the Patents Court-specific disclosure modifications, so for more detail you may want to search the Patents Court Guide and PD 63. [2][3]

results.name: TCC Experts
results.question: How does the Technology and Construction Court handle expert evidence?

unfiltered.answer:
In the TCC, expert evidence is often needed and used, but the parties and the court are expected to make effective and proportionate use of experts from the earliest pre-action stage to trial, and the scope of expert evidence must be limited to what is necessary for the case. [6]

The TCC Guide says expert evidence is evidence on technical or scientific matters, will generally include the expert’s opinions, and its quality depends on the expert’s experience, qualifications, and the factual material used. [1]

Expert evidence is governed in detail by CPR Part 35, which says it must be restricted to what is reasonably required to resolve the proceedings, experts have an overriding duty to help the court, and no party may call an expert or rely on an expert’s report without the court’s permission. [2]

The TCC considers the way expert evidence is given at the PTR, and where there are multiple experts the court may direct different methods, including sequential evidence or concurrent evidence (“hot-tubbing”). [7]

The TCC Guide also warns parties to avoid incurring the costs of expert evidence on uncontroversial matters before the first CMC, because the court may later direct joint appointments or limit expert evidence. [8]

results.name: KB Division Listing
results.question: What are the King's Bench Division Guide's provisions on listing?

unfiltered.answer:
The King's Bench Division Guide says the KB Civil List covers all matters not in the Media and Communications List, including trials, preliminary questions or issues ordered to be tried, and proceedings to commit for contempt of court. [1]

It also says the majority of trials fall within the KB Civil List, and if a jury trial is ordered outside the Media and Communications List, the normal Civil List procedure is followed, but a fixed trial date will be given. [1]

The Guide explains that the Royal Courts of Justice creates particular difficulties for fixing trial dates, so the Chancery and King's Bench Divisions use a different approach to listing trials there. [2]

Once a listing appointment has been given, all listing matters are under the control and supervision of the Judge in Charge of the King's Bench Civil List or, where relevant, the Judge in charge of the Media and Communications List. [3]

Any request to change the trial window, whether by consent or otherwise, must be dealt with by the Judge in charge of the relevant list or a judge nominated by them, not by a Master. [3]

If an application to extend or change a trial window is made to a Master, it will be transferred to the Judge in charge of the List, and such applications should be made to that Judge and notified to the KB Listing office to avoid delay. [4]

For urgent and short applications, the USAL is listed before all Masters on a rota basis every day from 10.30am to 1.00pm and from 2.00pm to 4.30pm unless otherwise indicated. [5]

Short applications of no more than 30 minutes may be listed in the USAL, but applications estimated to take more than 30 minutes should be listed as a MA instead. [6]

Asbestos List cases are listed in accordance with the Mesothelioma Practice Direction (PD49B), and the only permitted supplemental headings are the heading required by PD49B and the marking “limited life expectancy” where applicable. [7]

For trial listing, the Master gives directions for the trial window, venue, mode of trial, listing category, estimated length, and service of the order on the King's Bench Judges Listing Office, which then notifies the parties of a listing appointment. [9]

The Guide says the listing appointment will usually be within 6 weeks of the order being sealed, or 3 weeks for mesothelioma liability trials. [9]

If you want, I can also pull out just the rules on trial windows, the USAL, or the Asbestos List.

results.name: CPR Appeal Time Limits (should NOT filter)
results.question: What are the time limits for filing an appeal under the CPR?
results.expected_category: Civil Procedure Rules and Practice Directions

unfiltered.answer:
Under CPR Part 52, an appellant’s notice must usually be filed within 21 days, and the time runs from the date the lower court made the decision, not from the date the formal order was issued. [2]

There are sometimes different time limits for statutory appeals, so the relevant prescribed time limit should be checked. [2]

For certain contempt proceedings, the application for permission to appeal must be made within 28 days of the date the court provides reasons for its decision, and for appeals from the Court of Appeal to the Supreme Court in those proceedings, within 28 days after the Court of Appeal’s decision. [7]

If you want, I can also give the separate CPR time limits for a respondent’s notice or for a specific type of appeal.

filtered.answer:
The sources available do not directly give the general time limit for filing an appellant’s notice under CPR Part 52. [3]

What they do say is that rule 52.12 sets the time limits for filing an appellant’s notice at the appeal court, and rule 52.13 sets the time limits for filing a respondent’s notice at the appeal court. [3]

For appeals by way of case stated, the appellant must file the appellant’s notice at the appeal court within 10 days of the date of the case stated by the court. [16]

For certain contempt appeals, an application for permission to appeal must be made within 28 days of the date on which the court provides reasons for its decision, or within 28 days after the Court of Appeal’s decision, depending on the route. [3]

results.name: Cross-Court Disclosure (should NOT filter)
results.question: How do the different court guides approach disclosure differently?

unfiltered.answer:
The CPR/Practice Direction position in the sources is that standard disclosure under PD 31A requires a reasonable search, a list of documents, and the search should be proportionate to the circumstances. [5]  

The Chancery Guide says that disclosure in proceedings issued in the B&PCs is dealt with further in Chapter 7, and it reminds parties that ChD B&PCs London and the listed District Registries are subject to PD 57AD. [1]  

The Commercial Court Guide says PD 57AD applies to most Commercial Court proceedings, with deadlines for disclosure before the CMC, but not to the Admiralty Court or to cases in the Shorter Trials Scheme or Flexible Trials Scheme unless ordered. [3]  

The Commercial Court Guide also says the Disclosure Review Document should be simple and concise, with Issues for Disclosure kept within the PD 57AD definition and unnecessary proliferation of Models for Extended Disclosure avoided. [4]  

The TCC Guide says disclosure in the TCC generally is subject to PD 57AD, but there are exceptions for Public Procurement claims, Shorter and Flexible Trials Scheme proceedings, and fixed costs regime proceedings. [11]  

The TCC Guide also says CPR Part 31 and PD 31B continue to apply to Public Procurement claims, and it specifically points parties to separate e-disclosure protocol guidance for those cases. [11]  

So the main difference shown by these sources is that the court guides mainly diverge on when PD 57AD applies and on court-specific procedural guidance, while the CPR source in the materials describes the general standard disclosure framework. [1]
